lines.text: Somewhere a guy has decided he'll just run for it. There's always one guy.
lines.note: Varies the star "Coat weather. Except for the one guy in shorts. There's always one guy." Same frame and closer, new image: the man who'd rather sprint through the rain than carry an umbrella. Neighbors the vetoed "Big day for the man who refuses to own an umbrella" but turns on the sprint, not on proving a point.

lines.text: Umbrellas work a few days a year and lean in a corner the rest. Great union.
lines.note: Varies the star "Hours of carrying for minutes of use. Still a good deal." (what an umbrella gives for what it gets), told as a job the way VOICE level 10 asks. The vetoed "A rainy day with a tea break. Union rules." put the union on the rain. This one puts it on the umbrella's contract.

lines.text: Doormats everywhere are about to have a very long day.
lines.note: Varies the star "Seat belt buckles everywhere are turning into branding irons." Same shape: an object all over town that the weather is about to ruin. Rain version: every wet shoe gets wiped on it. Works under rain from a time and under a wet start.

lines.text: Rain is just snow that stopped trying.
lines.note: Flips the star "Snow is just rain that cares about presentation." Same definition frame turned around, so rain gets the insult. Short and works in any season. Risk: it may read as too close a mirror of the star.

lines.text: The Farmer's Almanac called this snow too. A year ago, for 'the Northeast.'
lines.note: Varies the star "Horoscopes predict the future too. Not one has ever mentioned pants." Another forecaster that can't give the practical part. The Almanac really does print winter predictions a year ahead, by broad region. A very American reference, but it might be lost on readers outside the US.

lines.text: Kids will love it. Driveways, less so.
lines.note: Flips the star "The kids won't take the news well." (snow stopping) for snow on the way. Kids are happy, the shoveling falls on the driveway. Two beats, no restatement.

lines.text: Snow is lovely for about an hour. After that, it's a parking problem.
lines.note: Varies the star "The novelty lasts an hour. The snow lasts all day." Same arc from charm to chore, ending on a new and very concrete chore.

lines.text: Every dad on the block is about to become a road-salt expert.
lines.note: Varies the star "The one forecast that makes adults text each other in capital letters." Same frame: how grown-ups act about snow. New image: the dad who suddenly has opinions on salt. The salt trucks are live ("so the salt trucks can feel useful"), but this is a different joke.

lines.text: A dishwasher sort of day. Rinse cycle first, then dry.
lines.note: Varies the star "Today is a microwave burrito. Warm in the middle, cold at both ends." Same frame: the day as a household appliance, with its two parts as the punchline. It's an image of wet-then-dry, not a restatement.

lines.text: 'Rain before seven, clear by eleven.' Close enough, for folklore.
lines.note: Varies the star "Folk wisdom nailed one month and retired." (April showers): a weather saying that is roughly right, for once. The line quotes the saying, so it needs no outside setup. 'Close enough' covers any dry-from time.

lines.text: For once I can say 'it'll pass' and mean it.
lines.note: Flips the star "I'd say 'it'll pass,' but I'm honest." (rain that lasts). With a dry finish, the screen finally gets to use the line it held back. This is about honesty, not the dead 'always right' move.

lines.text: Later, the umbrella's just a wet stick you carry around for company.
lines.note: Varies the star "After that, you're just carrying {GP} around for company." (arc_warmer) with the umbrella once the rain stops. Points to the time drawing, so it reads without the sentence.

lines.text: Later someone out there will say 'oh, that's nice' out loud. To nobody.
lines.note: Varies the star "Later you'll pull it on and say 'ah, that's better'. Out loud." The target is a stranger, not the reader, so it fits On. 'To nobody' adds a beat.

lines.text: An app needs a whole graph for this. I just draw less clothing.
lines.note: Varies the star "All of tomorrow in a few words. Some need a five-minute voice memo to say less." Same frame: the screen says it more briefly than the others. True to the screen: the warmer drawing has a lighter outfit (T-shirt and shorts count as one, so warmer always means a change).

lines.text: A wardrobe change partway through. The weather thinks it's a pop star.
lines.note: Varies the star "Two outfit changes in one day. Very pop star of you." The vanity moves from the reader to the weather, which makes it On. The original is live in daytime offon, so the owner may find it too close.

lines.text: I'll take credit for the warm part. The cold start was someone else's idea.
lines.note: Varies the star "I'll take the credit for that." (c_relief). The new twist splits the day: the screen claims the good half and disowns the bad half. Risk: taking credit is live several times in daytime pools.

lines.text: Weather this dependable could sell life insurance.
lines.note: Varies the star "Weather this average could get a job in middle management." Same frame (weather this X could get job Y), new job: steady, reliable, a bit dull.

lines.text: I could do this forecast in sleep mode. I do most things in sleep mode.
lines.note: Varies the star "The one forecast I could do in my sleep." The new twist is true to the device: TRMNL sleeps between refreshes, so the screen admits it is barely awake most of the time. Self-deprecating, not smug.

lines.text: One picture from morning to night. I finally know how museum guards feel.
lines.note: Varies the star "Somewhere a screen is showing a Monet. And all you get is this." (screen vs. art). A steady day means one drawing all day, so the screen feels like a guard stuck with one painting. It touches the drawings, which the owner has asked to do less.

lines.text: Every fortune cookie promises big changes ahead. Not this forecast.
lines.note: Varies the star "Horoscopes predict the future too. Not one has ever mentioned pants." Another fake predictor, this time with its stock line ('big changes ahead') proved wrong by a one-outfit day. Not 'more of today': the joke is the cookie's promise.

lines.text: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting. It's swiping right.
lines.replaces: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting.
lines.note: Punchline a: picking a forecast like a dating profile, the best-looking one wins. 83 characters.

lines.text: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting. It's asking Dad.
lines.replaces: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting.
lines.note: Punchline b: Mom said no, so ask the parent who says yes. Everyone knows the move. 80 characters.

lines.text: Checking apps until one says sunny isn't forecasting. It's shaking a Magic 8 Ball.
lines.replaces: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting.
lines.note: Punchline c, with the setup reworded so it fits: you shake until you get the answer you want. 82 characters.

lines.text: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting. It's casting.
lines.replaces: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting.
lines.note: Punchline d: holding auditions for tomorrow's weather and giving the part to the best-looking one. Shortest (77), but the most abstract; it may need a beat.

lines.text: Checking three apps and trusting the nicest isn't forecasting. It's flattery with radar.
lines.replaces: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting.
lines.note: Punchline e: the app is just telling people what they want to hear, with maps added. 'Trusting' replaces 'believing' to save room, but at 88 characters it's still over the owner's 'too long' mark.

lines.text: Look all you want. That outfit gets less attention once you're in it.
lines.note: For the screen without the sentence: 'that outfit' points straight at the drawings, so nothing above is needed. Same cruelty as the star, shorter and clearer (69).

lines.text: This is that outfit's big moment. Once you put it on, nobody looks.
lines.note: Second angle: the drawing is the outfit's peak, and wearing it ends its career. Also points at the drawings, 67 characters.

lines.text: Some people trust the porch thermometer. It hangs in full sun and always says shorts.
lines.replaces: Some people trust only their porch thermometer. It's been in direct sun since 1993.
lines.note: Clearer: shows the result (it always reads warm) in clothing terms, the screen's own field. 85 characters.

lines.text: Some people trust the porch thermometer. In full sun, it hasn't felt winter since 1993.
lines.replaces: Some people trust only their porch thermometer. It's been in direct sun since 1993.
lines.note: Keeps the owner's 1993 and states the result: in direct sun it never registers cold, so their forecast is never wrong in the right direction. 87 characters, just over the mark.

lines.text: Some people trust the porch thermometer over me. It sits in full sun. Total optimist.
lines.replaces: Some people trust only their porch thermometer. It's been in direct sun since 1993.
lines.note: Makes it a rivalry: the screen loses to a sun-baked thermometer, and 'optimist' means it always reads too warm, without explaining the joke. 85 characters.
